questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a protected connection prevents
questions.learningObjective: Identify what an encrypted transport protects
questions.stem: A depot supervisor wants to know exactly what an encrypted link between two offices stops an outsider on the public route from doing.

options.text: Reading or altering the message content while the link crosses the public route between the two offices
Reading what the receiving office stores on its own file server once the message has been delivered
options.misconception: assumes the tunnel keeps protecting data after it lands

options.text: Installing software on the receiving office's workstations by copying the encrypted message across
options.misconception: believes copied ciphertext can run code on the far side

options.text: Impersonating a supervisor to the staff rota system after the message has been received and opened
options.misconception: treats transport encryption as proof of who the sender was

questions.explanation: Encryption on the link protects content while it travels only. It does not protect what the receiving office stores afterwards, and it does not prove who sat at the other end.
questions.hint: Think about the moment the data reaches the far end.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The reach of a protected connection
questions.learningObjective: Interpret coverage figures for a protected link
questions.stem: The transport tunnel protects 42 of the 64 links on a regional network, and a planner reports that the network is now fully protected because the tunnel is working.

options.text: The report is right, because a working tunnel protects every link it touches once it is switched on
options.misconception: assumes one tunnel covers every link on the estate

options.text: The report overstates the coverage, because only the 42 tunneled links are covered and 22 links remain exposed
The report is right, because 42 protected links are more than half the estate and that is the accepted threshold
options.misconception: treats majority coverage as if it were full coverage

options.text: The report is wrong for an unrelated reason, because regional networks cannot carry encrypted tunnels at all
options.misconception: claims the estate cannot carry encrypted tunnels at all

questions.explanation: The tunnel protects the links it actually covers, which is 42 of 64. Twenty-two links remain uncovered, so calling the network fully protected mistakes partial protection for complete protection.
questions.hint: Count the links the tunnel does not cover.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Extending a private network over a public route
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a tunnel extends private reach across public infrastructure
questions.stem: Explain in your own words why carrying depot traffic across a public route inside a tunnel extends a private network without making the public route private.

answer.exemplar: A tunnel gives traffic from the private sites a usable address and path over infrastructure the organisation does not control, so remote sites appear directly reachable from inside. The cable, the exchange and the path stay public and shared, and anyone on that path can still see routing and timing, so the public route is not made private, only the carried traffic is kept to the tunnel's two endpoints.

questions.explanation: The tunnel carries private-site packets across the public route so remote sites behave as if adjacent. The route itself stays public and shared; only traffic inside the tunnel is confined to its two ends.
questions.hint: Separate the addressing from the physical route.

questions.topic: The trust a tunnel still requires
questions.learningObjective: Calculate key counts for mutually authenticated tunnel endpoints
questions.stem: A planner must build mutually authenticated tunnel endpoints for 6 depots, and each depot needs 2 keys, one held at the depot and one at the central control room. How many keys must be issued in total?
questions.explanation: Each of the 6 depots holds one key at its own end and one at control, so every depot consumes 2 keys. Six depots times 2 keys each gives 12 keys, and the tunnel does not work until all 12 are present.
questions.hint: Multiply the number of depots by keys per depot.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Limiting how far a foothold reaches
questions.learningObjective: Judge the reach of a foothold from captured evidence

stimulus.body: An intruder gained a foothold on a maintenance terminal in the signalling depot at 02:14. The terminal can reach the depot file share and the shift roster service, but a packet capture shows no session to the ticketing cluster, the timetable database or the public web gateway. The planning desk has already asked whether the network is compromised.

questions.stem: Given this report, what can the planner conclude about how far the foothold reaches?

options.text: The foothold has the same reach as any member of staff on the depot network
options.misconception: treats one compromised host as a whole-network compromise

options.text: The breach is still spreading silently because the capture simply missed early traffic
options.misconception: assumes unseen traffic means unseen access

options.text: The foothold is limited to the depot segment it landed in, and the rest of the estate was not reached
The timetable database must be compromised because it shares a name with the shift roster service
options.misconception: infers compromise from a shared name

questions.explanation: Reach is confirmed only to two depot services and no session is seen elsewhere, so the foothold looks contained. A capture is weaker than a confirmed session, but does not support wider reach.
questions.hint: Separate what was reached from what was not.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: How much of an estate a zone removes
questions.learningObjective: Compute blast radius and state the isolation assumption
questions.stem: A depot estate of 120 hosts is split so that a compromised zone of 40 hosts is isolated from the remaining 80. First, state how many hosts the zone removes from an intruder's reach; second, state what that figure assumes about the isolation rule.

options.text: It removes 40 hosts, and the figure assumes nothing further because isolation is always complete
options.misconception: assumes any zone boundary is perfectly airtight

options.text: It removes 80 hosts, and the figure assumes the remaining hosts cannot reach the zone at all
options.misconception: reverses the zone and the remainder when counting hosts

options.text: It removes 120 hosts, and the figure assumes the whole estate is inside the zone boundary
options.misconception: counts the whole estate as if it all sat inside the zone

options.text: It removes 40 hosts, and the figure assumes the isolation rule blocks every path out of that zone

questions.explanation: The 40 hosts inside the zone are removed from reach; the other 80 are not. The figure is only meaningful if the isolation rule blocks every path out of the zone, which is the assumption to check.
questions.hint: Count the zone, then name what the count assumes.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The first matching rule decides
questions.learningObjective: Predict which rule governs under first-match filtering
questions.stem: A route filter holds a rule allowing any traffic from the depot to the whole estate, listed above a rule denying access to the ticketing cluster. Which rule governs a packet to that cluster?

options.text: The deny rule, because a deny always overrides an allow regardless of the order of the list
options.misconception: believes deny rules always win over earlier allows

options.text: The allow rule, because the first rule that matches decides the outcome and it is listed first
The deny rule, because the list is scanned from the bottom and the last match is applied
options.misconception: thinks the last matching rule is the one that counts

options.text: Neither rule, because a packet needs a match from every rule in the list before it is allowed
options.misconception: assumes all rules must match before a decision

questions.explanation: The first matching rule decides, and the allow is listed first, so it governs and the deny is never reached. The tempting answer assumes deny rules hold priority, which ordinary packet filters do not grant.
questions.hint: Look at which rule the filter meets first.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The order of checks a client makes
questions.learningObjective: Read a handshake log in the correct check order
questions.stem: A client log shows that cipher suites were listed, then a server certificate was presented and checked against the expected host name, then a session key was agreed, then a finished message arrived. Which sequence does the log show?

options.text: Certificate checking came after the finished message, so the key was trusted before the name was checked
options.misconception: reads the log backwards and inverts the order

options.text: Only the cipher list and the finished message were checked, and the certificate was never examined
options.misconception: assumes the certificate entry is decorative

options.text: Name checking happened before the key was agreed, so the peer was identified before any key was trusted
The certificate, the key agreement and the finished message all happened at the same instant
options.misconception: treats handshake steps as simultaneous

questions.explanation: The log puts the name check before key agreement, the safe order, since identity is settled before a key is trusted. The tempting answer reads the log backwards and claims the key came first.
questions.hint: Read the log entries in the order printed.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a protected connection prevents
questions.learningObjective: Contrast what a protected connection covers with what it leaves open
questions.stem: Describe the difference between what a protected connection stops and what it leaves untouched, using an example from a depot moving shift data to a control room.

answer.exemplar: A protected connection secures the path between the depot and the control room, so an outsider on the shared public route cannot read the shift data or change it unnoticed while it travels. Everything at the ends is unchanged by that protection: the depot machine could still be compromised, the control room could still be reached by someone with valid credentials, and the shift file is still stored on the control room's own disk in whatever form the service keeps it.

questions.explanation: A protected connection stops anyone on the shared route reading or altering shift data in transit. It leaves untouched what happens at either end, including who may receive it and what control stores later.
questions.hint: Name the path that is protected and the ends that are not.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Extending a private network over a public route
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish extended reach from a privatised route

stimulus.body: A small operator wants the three small depots to reach the central timetable server as if they sat on the same private network. The public route between them carries other traffic the operator does not own or control. The tunnels will be authenticated at both ends, but the operator notes that the carrier still sees routing information.

questions.stem: Given these facts, what does the operator's plan actually achieve, and what does it leave exposed?

options.text: It makes the public route private for the operator, because every byte on that route now belongs to the operator
options.misconception: believes tunnelling privatises the shared infrastructure

options.text: It protects the depots from each other, because the tunnel separates one depot's traffic from another's
options.misconception: thinks the tunnel isolates the three depots from each other

options.text: It stops the carrier from learning which depot is talking to the timetable server
options.misconception: assumes address visibility disappears with the tunnel

options.text: It extends private reach to the depots while the public route and the carrier's view of routing stay as they were

questions.explanation: The tunnel gives the depots a private path to the server over shared infrastructure. It neither privatises the carrier's route nor hides which sites are talking, so the tempting claim overstates the result.
questions.hint: Ask what the carrier still learns from the route.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The trust a tunnel still requires
questions.learningObjective: Identify the endpoint identity check and its dependency
questions.stem: Two depots join a tunnel to the control room, and each end must prove its identity before the tunnel carries traffic. First, name the check that establishes which depot is at the far end; second, say what that check depends on.

options.text: Certificate validation against a trusted authority, which depends on the certificate chain rooting in a trusted store
Password entry at the depot console, which depends on the depot staff remembering the shared secret
options.misconception: treats a shared passphrase as endpoint identity

options.text: Route selection by the carrier, which depends on the carrier choosing a path that avoids other networks
options.misconception: believes the carrier's routing proves identity

options.text: Bandwidth measurement across the link, which depends on the tunnel being wide enough to carry the depot's data
options.misconception: confuses link capacity with endpoint identity

questions.explanation: Endpoint identity comes from validating a certificate rooted in a trusted store. The tempting answers substitute a passphrase, routing or capacity, none of which binds a name to a key.
questions.hint: Think about what binds a name to a key.

questions.topic: Limiting how far a foothold reaches
questions.learningObjective: State the boundary of a foothold in terms of reachable systems
questions.stem: A foothold on a maintenance laptop in the signalling depot lets an intruder reach the depot printer and the local controller. Which statement best describes the limit the intruder has reached?

options.text: The limit is the whole authority, because the depot laptop is joined to the staff network
options.misconception: assumes network membership grants estate-wide reach

options.text: The limit is the signalling system itself, because the local controller controls the points
options.misconception: assumes one controller controls the whole signalling system

options.text: The limit is the depot segment, because the printer and controller are the only systems in reach
There is no limit yet, because the intruder has not been seen moving laterally
options.misconception: equates not seeing movement with having no reach

questions.explanation: Reach is bounded by what the foothold can actually reach, here the printer and the local controller. Not observing movement is not a boundary, so the tempting claim of no limit is unsupported.
questions.hint: List the systems the intruder demonstrably reached.

questions.topic: How much of an estate a zone removes
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the estate reduction produced by an isolated zone
questions.stem: An estate of 300 devices is split into four zones of 75. After a zone is isolated, an intruder in one zone is still able to reach 75 devices. Which figure shows how many devices the isolation actually removed from the intruder's reach?

options.text: 75 devices, because the intruder can still reach the devices inside the isolated zone
options.misconception: counts the zone itself as removed from reach

options.text: 300 devices, because isolating one zone removes every route in the estate
options.misconception: believes one zone cut disconnects the whole estate

options.text: 150 devices, because isolation always removes half of any estate
options.misconception: assumes a fixed half of the estate is always cut

options.text: 225 devices, because 300 minus the 75 still reachable leaves 225 out of reach

questions.explanation: The intruder still reaches 75 devices, so 300 minus 75 leaves 225 out of reach. The tempting answers count the zone as removed or remove the whole estate, and neither follows from the figures.
questions.hint: Subtract what is still reachable from the total.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The first matching rule decides
questions.learningObjective: Explain why rule order determines filtering outcome
questions.stem: Explain to a depot manager why the order in which filter rules are listed changes which traffic is actually permitted, even when the same rules are present.

answer.exemplar: Most filter lists are evaluated top down and the first rule that matches decides the packet's fate. If a broad allow for all depot traffic is placed above a narrow deny aimed at the ticketing cluster, every packet to that cluster matches the allow and the deny is never consulted, so the deny provides no protection at all. Moving the deny above the allow restores it, which shows that the content of the list is not enough; the order carries meaning and has to be reviewed whenever rules are added.

questions.explanation: A filter stops at the first matching rule and applies that outcome, so a broad allow above a narrow deny makes the deny unreachable. The same rules reordered give a different network.
questions.hint: Ask which rule a matching packet meets first.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The order of checks a client makes
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a failed certificate check in a client log

stimulus.body: Client log from a depot tablet: 09:02:11 negotiated version; 09:02:11 cipher list exchanged; 09:02:12 server certificate presented; 09:02:12 certificate rejected, name does not match host; 09:02:13 connection closed; no session key agreed.

questions.stem: According to this log, what did the client do correctly, and what happened as a result?

options.text: It checked the certificate name before agreeing a key, so the session ended without a key being established
It agreed a key first and then checked the name, so the security failure came after the key was live
options.misconception: reorders the log so the key comes first

options.text: It skipped name checking because the version and cipher list had already been agreed
options.misconception: treats early agreement as a reason to skip checks

options.text: It failed because the cipher list was empty, and the certificate was never relevant to the outcome
options.misconception: blames the cipher list and dismisses the certificate

questions.explanation: The log shows the certificate name checked and rejected, then the connection closed with no key agreed. That is the safe order, identity before key, so the tempting reordered reading misreads the record.
questions.hint: Find the last line that records a key.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a protected connection prevents
questions.learningObjective: Separate hidden content from observable session metadata
questions.stem: A depot link is protected by a tunnel that terminates at the central control room. First, state what an outsider on the shared route can still learn from the link; second, state what they cannot obtain.

options.text: They can read the message body and learn nothing else, and they cannot read the body once it is decrypted
options.misconception: conflates seeing the body with being able to read it

options.text: They can see that a session exists and its timing and size, and they cannot read the content
They can learn the route and the destination address, and they cannot learn which depot is involved
options.misconception: claims destinations are hidden while routes are visible

options.text: They can read everything and learn nothing, and they cannot read anything at all under any condition
options.misconception: claims total visibility and total blindness at once

questions.explanation: A protected link hides content but not that a session exists, nor its timing or size. The tempting answers claim the body is readable, that destinations are hidden, or that visibility is total and absent.
questions.hint: Separate what is hidden from what is merely obscure.

questions.topic: Extending a private network over a public route
questions.learningObjective: State what a tunnel changes about reach between private sites
questions.stem: An operator tunnels three remote depots to a central server across infrastructure operated by a third party. What does the tunnel actually change about the path?

options.text: It replaces the third party's route with a physically separate cable reserved for the operator
options.misconception: believes tunnelling reserves dedicated physical capacity

options.text: It gives the third party the ability to decrypt the depot traffic because the route belongs to them
options.misconception: confuses route ownership with decryption ability

options.text: It stops the third party from seeing which destinations the depots reach on the shared route
options.misconception: assumes tunnelling removes destination visibility

options.text: It carries private-site traffic across the shared route so the remote sites appear directly reachable

questions.topic: The trust a tunnel still requires
questions.learningObjective: Calculate key consumption across failed tunnel attempts
questions.stem: A depot client made 5 failed attempts to establish a tunnel before one succeeded, and each attempt used 2 keys drawn from a pool of 40. How many keys were consumed by the failed attempts?

options.text: 8 keys, because four attempts were made before the fifth succeeded and each used 2 keys
options.misconception: off by one attempt in the count

options.text: 10 keys, because 5 attempts times 2 keys per attempt gives 10 keys used
20 keys, because the successful attempt also consumed 2 keys from the same pool
options.misconception: counts the successful attempt as well

options.text: 40 keys, because each attempt consumed the whole pool before failing
options.misconception: assumes each attempt exhausted the key pool

questions.explanation: Each failed attempt used 2 keys, and 5 attempts times 2 gives 10 consumed, leaving 30 in the pool. The tempting answer divides 40 by 5, which measures keys per attempt rather than keys spent.
questions.hint: Multiply attempts by keys used per attempt.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Limiting how far a foothold reaches
questions.learningObjective: Explain why segmentation limits a foothold's reach
questions.stem: Explain why a foothold inside a segmented depot estate should be assumed to have a smaller reach than the number of hosts sitting in the same zone.

answer.exemplar: A zone is not just a label on a group of machines; it is a group of machines that share a permitted path to each other and are cut off from other zones by a rule. An intruder who lands on one machine in a zone inherits that zone's permitted reach and nothing more, provided the boundary rule actually blocks the other directions. That is why the useful measure of a foothold is the set of systems reachable from its own segment, which is normally a small fraction of the hosts the intruder could have touched if the estate had no segmentation at all. The caveat is that segmentation only holds if the rule between the zones is enforced in every direction and no shared service quietly bridges the two sides.

questions.explanation: Segmentation puts a rule between zones so traffic cannot cross without explicit permission. A foothold reaches only the systems its zone can reach, usually fewer than every host on that segment.
questions.hint: Ask what the zone boundary actually blocks.

options.text: The message text is exposed because the headers are visible on the route
options.misconception: treats visible headers as exposed content

options.text: The content is protected while the existence and timing of sessions remain visible
The whole connection is unencrypted because some fields are readable to the interceptor

questions.learningObjective: Diagnose an unreachable deny rule and propose a fix
questions.stem: Two rules sit in a filter: rule 1 allows all traffic from the depot network, rule 2 denies traffic to the ticketing cluster. First, state which rule decides a packet to that cluster; second, state the change that would make rule 2 effective.

options.text: Rule 2 decides it, and moving rule 2 to the top of the list would make rule 1 effective
options.misconception: reverses both the decision and the proposed fix

options.text: Rule 1 decides it, and deleting rule 1 would make rule 2 effective
options.misconception: proposes deleting a rule instead of reordering

options.text: Rule 1 decides it, and moving rule 2 above rule 1 would make rule 2 effective
Both rules decide it, and applying both outcomes together would make rule 2 effective
options.misconception: assumes every matching rule is applied

questions.explanation: The first match decides, so rule 1 permits the packet and rule 2 is never consulted. Moving rule 2 above rule 1 restores the deny, while the tempting answers reverse the decision or apply every match.

questions.learningObjective: Order the checks that precede trust in a server
questions.stem: Before a depot client trusts a server it has never met, which check must come first in a correct handshake sequence?

options.text: Confirming the server certificate matches the name the client intended to reach
Agreeing the session key, so that the checks afterwards travel inside the protected channel
options.misconception: puts key agreement before any identity check

options.misconception: treats a valid date as proof of identity

options.misconception: treats a usable cipher list as a security decision

options.misconception: claims the two figures cannot both be true

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The reach of a protected connection
questions.learningObjective: Explain why protection is per path rather than per software
questions.stem: Explain why a protected connection between a depot and a control room does not protect the depot's other links, even though both use the same tunnel software.

answer.exemplar: A tunnel is a property of a path between two specific endpoints, not a feature of the software installed on either end. If the depot's rota system reaches the control room through the tunnel, then exactly that connection is protected: the route it takes, the identity of the far endpoint and the content in between. Another link from the same depot to a different service, over a different exchange or terminating at a different box, is a different path with different endpoints, and nothing about the first path's protection extends to it. The shared software merely means both links use the same implementation, and an implementation is reusable across as many paths as it is installed on.

questions.explanation: A tunnel protects one path between one pair of endpoints. Other depot links terminate elsewhere or cross different infrastructure, so they are not on that path. Shared software does not widen a path.
questions.hint: Ask how many paths a single tunnel covers.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The first matching rule decides
questions.learningObjective: Compare additive and subtractive network changes
questions.stem: Describe how the estate-wide effect of a single broad allow rule differs from the effect of isolating one zone, and why the planner should prefer the zone.

answer.exemplar: A broad allow is additive. It says that everything the depot network may already reach becomes permitted, so it increases the amount of the estate an intruder or an error can touch, and it gives back nothing. An isolated zone is subtractive. Once the rule between two zones is enforced, the hosts on the far side of the boundary stop being reachable from the intruder's side, so the estate that an intruder can affect shrinks even though nothing new was enabled. The planner prefers the subtractive move because the property that matters after a foothold is not how much access a rule grants but how much access remains once an attacker is inside.

questions.explanation: A broad allow widens access without removing anything from reach. Isolating a zone removes a slice of the estate from an intruder's reach, shrinking what can be touched rather than widening it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the change adds reach or removes it.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: How much of an estate a zone removes
questions.learningObjective: Explain how path rules reduce reach without changing inventory
questions.stem: Explain why a zone can reduce an intruder's reach without reducing the number of machines the authority actually operates.

answer.exemplar: A zone is a rule about paths, not an inventory list. Moving a group of machines into a zone, or writing a rule that denies traffic between two groups of machines, changes which paths a packet may take while every machine keeps running, keeps its data and keeps its place in the timetable. The estate size stays exactly as it was. What changes is the set of machines an intruder standing in one group can reach, because the previously usable paths across the boundary are no longer permitted. That gap between the machines operated and the machines reachable is the practical benefit of segmentation, and it can grow without a single machine being switched off.

questions.explanation: A zone changes which paths are permitted, not how many machines exist. If the boundary blocks the routes an intruder used, machines behind it become unreachable yet stay in service, so the counts differ.
questions.hint: Ask about paths, not about machines.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The trust a tunnel still requires
questions.learningObjective: Explain the residual trust a tunnel places in its far endpoint
questions.stem: Explain why a tunnel that authenticates both ends still depends on the trust placed in the far endpoint's key.

answer.exemplar: A mutually authenticated tunnel proves that the machine at the far end of the link is the machine that was enrolled, because the handshake only completes when both sides present keys that match what was registered in advance. That is a statement about possession, not about conduct. The remote depot might still be running an unpatched operating system, might have been phished into handing over its key, or might have been taken over by someone who now holds it legitimately from the tunnel's point of view. Every byte that arrives through the tunnel is trusted on the strength of that possession, so the tunnel's protection is exactly as good as the key custody at the far end. This is why the identity check is worth doing properly: it does not make the endpoint safe, it only makes sure that traffic is coming from the endpoint you think it is.

questions.explanation: Authentication proves the far end holds the key it claims, not that it is honest. Everything the tunnel protects is trusted as it arrives, so a compromised far endpoint can read and alter it.
questions.hint: Ask what an identity check actually proves.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The order of checks a client makes
questions.learningObjective: Separate channel encryption from peer identity verification
questions.stem: Explain why a client that skips the certificate name check still ends up with a protected channel, and why that is not the same as having a safe session.

answer.exemplar: Encryption and certificate validation are separate properties of a connection. A client that verifies only that the certificate is well formed, or skips verification entirely, will still negotiate an algorithm and a key, and the bytes on the route will still be unreadable to anyone watching. That is why a session can look perfectly protected and still be dangerous. The missing check is the one that binds the certificate to the name the client asked for, and without it the client cannot tell the legitimate depot server from an impostor that answered first with its own certificate. The encrypted channel then protects the impostor's conversation rather than the real one, which is the opposite of what the protection is supposed to achieve.

questions.explanation: Without the name check a client can still negotiate strong keys and encrypt the channel, so bytes stay unreadable. But it never established which peer it reached, so it could apply to an impostor.
questions.hint: Ask whether the client knows who it reached.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The first matching rule decides
questions.learningObjective: Explain how adding a rule can weaken existing protections
questions.stem: A depot manager asks why adding one more broad allow rule to the filter may reduce the protection the estate already has.

options.text: Because a longer list makes the filter slower, and slow filters let traffic through unchecked
options.misconception: links list length to correctness by speed

options.text: Because the new rule is matched first for some packets and may make an existing deny unreachable
Because each rule consumes a key, and too many rules exhaust the key pool
options.misconception: invents a key cost for filter rules

options.text: Because rules only take effect when a full set of twenty is present
options.misconception: believes rules require a minimum count

questions.explanation: A new broad rule placed above existing denies is matched first for the traffic it covers and makes those denies unreachable. The tempting answers blame speed, invent a per-rule key cost or demand a minimum rule count, none of which applies.
questions.hint: Ask which rule a matching packet reaches first.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Limiting how far a foothold reaches
questions.learningObjective: Count blocked entry paths from rule coverage
questions.stem: A test of 12 possible entry paths finds that 5 of them have no rule at all, 4 have a rule that blocks the attempt, and 3 have a rule that permits it. How many entry paths are blocked?

options.text: 5 paths, because only the paths with no rule are considered blocked
options.misconception: counts the missing rules and ignores the blocking ones

options.text: 4 paths, because only the paths with an explicit deny are counted as blocked
options.misconception: counts explicit denies and ignores the missing rules

options.text: 3 paths, because the paths with no rule are still reachable by default
options.misconception: treats a missing rule as open rather than blocked

options.text: 9 paths, because the 5 without a rule and the 4 blocked by a rule are both closed

questions.explanation: Paths with no rule and paths with a blocking rule are both closed, so 5 plus 4 gives 9 blocked and 3 permitted. The tempting answer of 3 counts the permitted paths and reverses the question.
questions.hint: Add the two groups that end in no access.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The order of checks a client makes
questions.learningObjective: Explain why peer name checking precedes key agreement
questions.stem: Explain in your own words why a client checks the peer name before it agrees a session key, rather than the other way round.

answer.exemplar: The key agreement is the moment the two ends decide that from here on they share a secret and that everything they say is protected with it. Whatever the client concludes about who the far end is at that moment governs the whole session afterwards, because the two are inseparable once the secret exists. If the name check happens after the key, a client that has spoken to the wrong server has already committed to the conversation and can only notice the mistake by reading on. Doing the name check first means the session is created only when the peer is the one the client intended to reach, and a failure at that point costs nothing but a refused connection.

questions.explanation: Agreeing a key fixes who the two ends are for the session, so a later check comes too late. Checking the name first means a session only forms with a peer the client identified.
questions.hint: Ask what becomes unchangeable once the key is agreed.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a protected connection prevents
questions.learningObjective: Count the segments left reachable by a zone boundary
questions.stem: A zone contains 8 link segments and the boundary blocks 6 of them from the general network. How many segments in that zone remain reachable from the general network?
questions.explanation: Eight segments minus the six blocked leaves 2 reachable from the general network. The tempting answer of 6 reports what was cut rather than what is still open, and 8 ignores the boundary entirely.
questions.hint: Subtract the blocked segments from the zone size.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The trust a tunnel still requires
questions.learningObjective: Identify the stated conditions for sending operational data

stimulus.body: The authority's handbook states that a remote depot shall not send operational data unless the far endpoint has presented a certificate that chains to an authority in the depot's own trust store, and unless the depot client has confirmed that the certificate names the host it dialled. It adds that if either condition fails, the connection shall be closed and the failure logged.

questions.stem: What does the handbook require before operational data may be sent?

options.text: That the connection is encrypted, since an encrypted channel already identifies the peer
options.misconception: believes encryption alone identifies the peer

options.text: That the depot client records the certificate expiry date and compares it with the timetable
options.misconception: substitutes expiry checking for chain and name checks

options.text: That the far endpoint is on the list of known depot addresses maintained by the control room
options.misconception: relies on an address list instead of a certificate check

options.text: That the certificate chains to a trusted authority and names the host the client dialled

questions.explanation: The handbook sets two conditions, a chain to a trusted authority and a name matching the host dialled. A failure closes it. The tempting answers substitute encryption, expiry checks or an address list.
questions.hint: Read the conditions the handbook states outright.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: How much of an estate a zone removes
questions.learningObjective: Compute and qualify the machines outside a foothold's reach
questions.stem: An isolated zone holds 90 of the authority's 540 machines. First, state how many machines remain outside the intruder's reach; second, state the assumption behind that figure.

options.text: 450 machines remain out of reach, assuming the boundary rule blocks every path out of the zone
90 machines remain out of reach, assuming the zone contains only machines already unreachable
options.misconception: counts the isolated zone as out of reach

options.text: 540 machines remain out of reach, assuming the intrusion has spread through the whole estate
options.misconception: assumes estate-wide compromise

options.text: 270 machines remain out of reach, assuming the boundary always removes exactly half the estate
options.misconception: applies an invented half-estate rule

questions.explanation: The intruder still reaches the 90 machines in its own zone, so 540 minus 90 leaves 450 out of reach, provided the boundary blocks every path out. The tempting answers count the wrong group.
questions.hint: Ask which machines the intruder can still touch.
